easy.prompt: What does a process control block (PCB) primarily store?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A list of every file ever opened on the system.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The entire contents of the process heap and stack.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only the program's machine code on disk.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Per-process kernel metadata such as registers, state, and scheduling info.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The PCB is the kernel's record for a process: identifiers, CPU context, memory pointers, and scheduling state—not a full memory dump.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Open files are tracked per process, but not as a global history of all system activity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Process memory lives in separate address-space structures; the PCB holds pointers and metadata, not full heaps.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Executable code is stored in files and mapped pages, not duplicated wholesale in the PCB.

easy.prompt: After a successful fork() in Unix, what does fork() return in the child?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The child's PID

choices.label: D
choices.body: The parent's PID

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: fork() returns 0 to the child and the child's PID to the parent; −1 indicates failure.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The child receives 0; the parent receives the new PID.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: −1 signals failure, not success in the child.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The parent gets the child's PID, not its own.

easy.prompt: A context switch between two processes requires the kernel to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Save and restore CPU register state and switch to the other process's address space.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Copy the entire disk image of each process.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Recompile both programs from source.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Flush every file on the system to disk.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Scheduling swaps the running context: register image, stack pointer, page tables or address-space ID, and related kernel bookkeeping.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Processes are not duplicated at the storage layer on each switch.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Executables are already loaded; switching is a runtime operation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Context switches do not require global filesystem sync.

easy.prompt: Threads in the same process typically share…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Nothing; each thread is a separate process

choices.label: B
choices.body: Independent copies of the entire heap only

choices.label: C
choices.body: Address space, open file descriptors, and signal disposition.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Separate private address spaces

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Threads are lightweight execution units within one process: they share memory and OS resources attached to that process.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Threads deliberately share process resources; processes do not.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Sharing is broader than heap copies and includes code, globals, and OS handles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes different processes, not threads in one process.

easy.prompt: On a single-core CPU, running multiple threads can still improve overall throughput when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Some threads block on I/O while others run.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All threads are CPU-bound and never block

choices.label: C
choices.body: Threads eliminate the need for the scheduler

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each thread must busy-wait on a lock

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Overlapping computation with I/O waits keeps the CPU busy; pure CPU-bound work on one core does not speed up with more threads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: With no blocking, one core cannot run threads in parallel—only interleaved.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: More threads increase scheduling work, not remove it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Busy-waiting wastes CPU time and hurts throughput.

easy.prompt: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Non-preemptive: a job runs until it finishes or blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Preemptive on every memory access

choices.label: C
choices.body: Identical to shortest-remaining-time-first

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always optimal for average turnaround time

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: FCFS runs jobs in arrival order without time-slice preemption, which can cause convoy effects behind long jobs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: FCFS does not preempt based on memory references.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SRTF preempts on remaining time; FCFS does not.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Long jobs at the front can inflate waiting time for everyone behind them.

easy.prompt: Round-robin scheduling requires defining…

choices.label: A
choices.body: That all jobs have equal memory footprints

choices.label: B
choices.body: A static priority that never changes

choices.label: C
choices.body: A time quantum (time slice).

choices.label: D
choices.body: The exact burst time of every job in advance

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: RR gives each ready job up to one quantum before moving it to the tail of the ready queue.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Memory size is unrelated to RR's time-slice rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Priorities are central to priority schedulers, not basic RR.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: RR is preemptive by time, not by known burst lengths.

easy.prompt: Non-preemptive Shortest Job First (SJF) minimizes which metric for a given set of jobs (all available at time 0)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Average waiting time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Maximum turnaround time for every job

choices.label: C
choices.body: CPU utilization on a multi-core machine only

choices.label: D
choices.body: Number of context switches in a real-time system with deadlines

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Among non-preemptive orders with known bursts, SJF is optimal for average waiting time; it is not optimal for every per-job metric.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A very short job last could still have high turnaround; SJF optimizes averages, not every max.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SJF is a uniprocessor ordering property here, not a multicore utilization guarantee.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Context switches and deadline feasibility are different objectives.

easy.prompt: A primary reason operating systems use virtual memory is to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Give each process a large, private address space while mapping only used pages to RAM.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Store all data only on the CPU stack

choices.label: C
choices.body: Guarantee zero page faults after startup

choices.label: D
choices.body: Make physical RAM unnecessary

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Virtual memory decouples logical addresses from physical frames, enabling protection, sharing, and demand loading.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Processes use heap, mappings, and files—not just the stack.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Demand paging causes faults when pages are first touched.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Virtual memory still backs hot pages with physical RAM.

easy.prompt: A page fault on a demand-paged system usually means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The disk is full so the OS must halt

choices.label: B
choices.body: The process has no valid page table

choices.label: C
choices.body: The referenced page is not currently mapped in physical memory (or permissions failed).

choices.label: D
choices.body: The CPU has failed permanently

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: A fault traps to the OS, which may load the page, grow the stack, or deliver a segmentation fault for illegal access.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Faults can occur for many reasons; full disk is one possible failure mode, not the definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: User processes have page tables; faults reference valid tables with missing or protected entries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Page faults are normal control events handled by the OS.

easy.prompt: In a paging system, a virtual address is commonly split into…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A page number and an offset within the page.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A process ID and thread ID only

choices.label: C
choices.body: An inode number and block offset only

choices.label: D
choices.body: A segment name and line number only

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The page number indexes the page table; the offset indexes a byte within the chosen frame.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Identifiers are not the standard virtual-address partition for paging.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inode/block pairs belong to file indexing, not CPU virtual addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That mixes segmentation terminology with unrelated line numbers.

easy.prompt: Internal fragmentation in paging refers to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Free space between unrelated processes on disk

choices.label: B
choices.body: Bytes lost when segments of different sizes are packed

choices.label: C
choices.body: Time wasted in the scheduler queue

choices.label: D
choices.body: Unused bytes within the last page allocated to a region.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: If a process needs slightly more than k pages, the final page may be only partly used—waste inside the page granularity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is not the usual definition of internal fragmentation in paging.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Variable-sized segments relate to segmentation/external fragmentation concepts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is scheduling delay, not memory fragmentation.

easy.prompt: In Unix-like systems, an inode primarily stores…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The directory path string as the canonical name

choices.label: B
choices.body: The user's password hash

choices.label: C
choices.body: File metadata (permissions, size, timestamps, block pointers) but not the file name.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The list of all running processes

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Directory entries map names to inode numbers; the inode holds on-disk structure for the file object itself.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Paths are resolved via directory entries; names live in directories, not inodes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Authentication data lives in system databases, not per-file inodes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Process tables are kernel structures unrelated to inodes.

easy.prompt: A directory entry in a typical Unix file system associates a file name with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The PID of the process that created the file

choices.label: B
choices.body: An inode number.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The file's entire data blocks inline

choices.label: D
choices.body: The physical sector of the disk motor

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Lookup reads the directory mapping name → inode, then loads metadata from the inode.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Creation PID is not the standard directory entry payload.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Directory entries are small; data blocks are referenced from the inode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Directories map names to inode indices, not hardware motor sectors.

easy.prompt: A critical section is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Code that accesses shared mutable state and must not run concurrently with other such code.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A region of virtual memory that is always read-only

choices.label: C
choices.body: The boot loader's first 512 bytes

choices.label: D
choices.body: Any function that performs I/O to disk

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Mutual exclusion protects critical sections so updates to shared data remain consistent.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Read-only mappings need no mutex for writers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is a disk layout artifact, not a synchronization concept.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: I/O alone does not define a critical section; sharing and mutation do.

easy.prompt: A mutex (lock) is used to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ensure at most one thread executes a protected critical section at a time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Increase parallelism by allowing unlimited concurrent writers

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replace the need for any page table

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sort ready-queue jobs by shortest burst time

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Locks serialize access so invariants on shared structures hold during updates.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Mutexes restrict concurrency to preserve correctness.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Memory translation is unrelated to locking.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is a scheduling policy, not mutual exclusion.

easy.prompt: Which condition is NOT required for deadlock in Coffman's classic four conditions?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Hold and wait

choices.label: B
choices.body: Circular wait

choices.label: C
choices.body: Mutual exclusion

choices.label: D
choices.body: Preemption of resources (resources can be forcibly taken away).

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait; preemption prevents deadlock by breaking hold-and-wait chains.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hold and wait is required for deadlock to arise.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Circular wait completes the cycle of waiting processes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Mutual exclusion is one of the four necessary conditions.

easy.prompt: Hold and wait means a process…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Must finish I/O before requesting the CPU

choices.label: B
choices.body: Releases all resources before requesting any

choices.label: C
choices.body: Keeps resources it already holds while waiting for additional resources.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Cannot block in the kernel

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Hold-and-wait allows partial allocation, which can create cycles when combined with other conditions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: I/O ordering is unrelated to resource hold-and-wait.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would violate hold-and-wait; some designs avoid deadlock by requiring atomic acquisition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Processes block routinely; hold-and-wait is about resources, not blocking itself.

easy.prompt: With programmed I/O (polling), the CPU…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Repeatedly checks a device status register until the operation completes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sleeps until the device sends an interrupt

choices.label: C
choices.body: Transfers data without ever touching device registers

choices.label: D
choices.body: Offloads all copying to another process's page table

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Polling keeps the CPU in a tight loop testing ready bits—simple but wasteful while waiting.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes interrupt-driven I/O, not polling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Programmed I/O explicitly uses device registers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Page tables are unrelated to device polling.

easy.prompt: Interrupt-driven I/O allows the CPU to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Guarantee devices need no buffers

choices.label: B
choices.body: Eliminate all device drivers

choices.label: C
choices.body: Do other work until the device signals completion.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Avoid handling trap frames in the kernel

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The device raises an interrupt when attention is needed, reducing busy-wait compared with pure polling.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Buffering is still required for speed mismatches.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Drivers still manage devices; interrupts are how they get CPU attention.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Interrupts enter the kernel via trap/interrupt handling.

medium.prompt: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) differs from non-preemptive SJF because SRTF…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Never preempts and runs jobs strictly in arrival order

choices.label: B
choices.body: Preempts the running job when a newly arrived job has shorter remaining time.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ignores remaining burst time and uses only static priorities

choices.label: D
choices.body: Requires jobs to perform I/O after exactly one time quantum

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: SRTF is preemptive SJF: the CPU may switch when a shorter job becomes ready.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes FCFS, not SRTF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SRTF is explicitly based on remaining time, not static priority alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: I/O patterns are not part of SRTF's definition.

medium.prompt: Priority inversion occurs when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A high-priority task waits indirectly because a low-priority task holds a needed lock.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A page fault replaces the wrong physical frame

choices.label: C
choices.body: The CPU runs idle while the ready queue is empty

choices.label: D
choices.body: All tasks run at the same priority

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: A medium-priority task can preempt the low-priority lock holder, delaying the high-priority waiter—classic inversion.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a memory-management error, unrelated to scheduling priorities.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is idleness, not inversion.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Equal priorities do not create inversion between high and low tasks.

medium.prompt: Multilevel feedback queues (MLFQ) often use priority aging to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Store executable code inside the ready queue nodes

choices.label: B
choices.body: Guarantee zero context switches

choices.label: C
choices.body: Eliminate the need for time quanta

choices.label: D
choices.body: Prevent starvation by gradually increasing the priority of long-waiting jobs.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Without aging, low-priority jobs may never run; boosting priority after waiting addresses fairness.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Queues hold scheduling entities, not program binaries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: MLFQ scheduling still context-switches between jobs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Lower levels still commonly use quanta similar to round robin.

medium.prompt: A zombie process in Unix is one that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Shares no memory with its parent after fork

choices.label: B
choices.body: Consumes maximum CPU in an infinite loop

choices.label: C
choices.body: Has exited but whose exit status has not yet been reaped by its parent.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Has no page table and cannot run user code

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The kernel retains a minimal PCB until wait() collects the exit code—hence 'zombie.'

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Memory sharing is unrelated to zombie state after exit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zombies are not running; they are terminated entries awaiting reap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zombies are dead processes, but the definition is about unreaped exit state.

medium.prompt: The exec family of system calls replaces…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only the parent process with a new child PID

choices.label: B
choices.body: The kernel's interrupt vector table

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every thread in the system with a single global stack

choices.label: D
choices.body: The current process image with a new program while keeping the same PID (in the same process).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: fork() duplicates; exec() loads a new executable into the calling process's address space.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: exec does not create a new PID; fork does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: exec affects user process memory, not CPU trap vectors globally.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: exec affects one process image, not all threads system-wide.

medium.prompt: Kernel-level threads are advantageous because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: They always use less memory than a single-threaded process

choices.label: B
choices.body: The kernel can schedule threads independently, even if one thread blocks in the kernel.

choices.label: C
choices.body: User code can ignore all synchronization

choices.label: D
choices.body: The kernel never needs to context-switch

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Blocking in the kernel on one user thread does not necessarily block all threads if they are kernel threads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Thread structures add overhead; the benefit is schedulability, not guaranteed smaller footprint.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Shared memory still requires locks regardless of thread model.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More kernel threads can mean more switching, not less.

medium.prompt: Copy-on-write (COW) after fork() is used to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Defer copying physical pages until one process writes, sharing read-only mappings initially.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Copy every page eagerly at fork time always

choices.label: C
choices.body: Prevent parent and child from ever sharing memory

choices.label: D
choices.body: Disable page tables in the child

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: COW marks shared pages read-only and copies a frame only on write, making fork() cheaper.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Eager copy is the opposite of COW's lazy strategy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: COW explicitly shares until a write occurs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Both processes need valid page tables with shared read-only mappings.

medium.prompt: The working set model approximates a process's demand by tracking…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Pages referenced in a recent time window (working set size/limit).

choices.label: B
choices.body: The number of threads in other processes

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every file name in the filesystem cache

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only pages never accessed since boot

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Thrashing can be reduced by ensuring enough frames to cover the working set of active pages.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Cross-process thread counts do not define a process's working set.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Working sets refer to virtual pages a process touches, not directory names.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cold pages are the opposite of the actively referenced working set.

medium.prompt: A translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches…

choices.label: A
choices.body: CPU microcode patches only

choices.label: B
choices.body: Recent virtual-to-physical translations to avoid full page-table walks.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Entire disk blocks for journaling

choices.label: D
choices.body: User passwords for authentication

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: On a TLB hit, the MMU finds the frame quickly; on a miss, the OS or hardware walks page tables.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Microcode is separate from per-address translation caching.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TLBs cache address translations, not filesystem journal blocks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Security credentials are unrelated to the MMU.

medium.prompt: A multi-level page table's main benefit is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Making every virtual address have the same page number

choices.label: B
choices.body: Sparse address spaces: only allocate inner tables for used virtual regions.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Eliminating all page faults

choices.label: D
choices.body: Removing the need for physical memory

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Single huge tables waste memory; hierarchical tables allocate pages of page-table entries on demand.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Page numbers vary with virtual addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Page faults still occur for demand paging and protection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Multi-level tables still map to physical frames.

medium.prompt: Effective memory access time with a TLB combines hit rate and costs. If a memory reference takes 100 ns, a TLB hit takes 1 ns extra, a TLB miss adds a 100 ns table walk, and TLB hit rate is 99%, the effective time is approximately…

choices.label: A
choices.body: 200 ns

choices.label: B
choices.body: 101 ns

choices.label: C
choices.body: 201 ns

choices.label: D
choices.body: 100 ns

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That would ignore the high hit rate and assume every access pays a full walk.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is the miss cost only, not the weighted average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That omits TLB overhead even on hits.

medium.prompt: Journaling in a file system is primarily intended to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Store data only in the CPU cache

choices.label: B
choices.body: Encrypt all file names with a per-user key

choices.label: C
choices.body: Eliminate the need for directories

choices.label: D
choices.body: Make crash recovery consistent by recording intended updates before applying them.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Write-ahead logging lets the system replay or undo partial operations after power loss.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Persistent files still live on block storage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Encryption is orthogonal to journaling's consistency goal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Namespaces still need directory structure.

medium.prompt: A hard link and a symbolic (soft) link differ because a hard link…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cannot reference files, only directories

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always points to a different inode with duplicate data blocks immediately

choices.label: C
choices.body: Requires the target file to be on a different file system

choices.label: D
choices.body: Adds another directory entry for the same inode, while a symlink stores a path string.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Hard links share the inode; symlinks are separate files containing a pathname that may dangle.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hard links typically reference files; symlinks can name paths broadly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Hard links share the inode; duplicate data is not created.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Hard links must be on the same file system; symlinks can cross mounts.

medium.prompt: A counting semaphore initialized to 1 can serve as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A replacement for virtual memory

choices.label: B
choices.body: A page-replacement policy

choices.label: C
choices.body: A disk scheduling elevator

choices.label: D
choices.body: A mutex if only one thread waits on it at a time and no owner tracking is required.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Binary semaphores can serialize access like locks, though mutexes often include ownership semantics.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Semaphores synchronize threads; they do not translate addresses.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Page replacement picks frames; semaphores coordinate threads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Elevator algorithms reorder disk requests, not thread admission.

medium.prompt: A monitor bundles…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only spinlocks with no waiting queues

choices.label: B
choices.body: CPU microcode and device firmware in one struct

choices.label: C
choices.body: A filesystem inode and disk superblock

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mutual exclusion with condition variables for wait/signal on shared state.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Monitors encapsulate data and operations so only one thread runs inside at a time, with condition queues for coordination.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Monitors rely on blocking and condition queues, not busy-wait alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That mixes unrelated low-level components.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Monitors are a concurrency construct, not on-disk metadata.

medium.prompt: Spinlocks are most appropriate when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Threads may sleep while holding the lock

choices.label: B
choices.body: The system is always single-core with long critical sections

choices.label: C
choices.body: The critical section is very short and the lock will not be held across blocking calls.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Page faults must be handled inside the critical section

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Spinning wastes CPU if waits are long or the holder blocks; short, non-blocking sections on multicore can favor spinlocks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sleeping while holding a spinlock would waste CPUs spinning for a long time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: On one core, spinning during long sections is especially wasteful.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Faults may block; spinlocks should not be held across blocking events.

medium.prompt: In the banker's algorithm, a state is safe if…

choices.label: A
choices.body: No process may request additional resources

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every process holds the maximum resources it might ever need

choices.label: C
choices.body: There exists an ordering in which every process can finish with currently available resources.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The system has detected a cycle in the wait-for graph

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Safety is a forecast: some sequence of completions releases enough resources for everyone to terminate.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Future requests are modeled via claim/max matrices; safety considers them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes allocation at the limit, not the definition of a safe sequence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A cycle suggests deadlock; safety is a preventive test before granting.

medium.prompt: A cycle in a resource-allocation graph indicates deadlock only if…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every resource has unlimited instances

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each resource in the cycle has a single instance (no multi-unit resources).

choices.label: C
choices.body: No process is waiting

choices.label: D
choices.body: All edges are request edges only with no assignment edges

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient; with single-instance resources, a cycle implies deadlock.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Unlimited instances break deadlock via cycles because requests can always be satisfied.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Deadlock requires waiting processes; no waiting means no deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Assignment edges show ownership; cycles need both assignment and request structure.

medium.prompt: Direct Memory Access (DMA) allows…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Disks to modify page tables without the OS

choices.label: B
choices.body: Devices to transfer data to or from memory without per-word CPU copying.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Processes to bypass all permission checks automatically

choices.label: D
choices.body: The CPU to execute user programs in device firmware

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: The CPU sets up DMA descriptors; the device moves bytes, then interrupts when done.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Page tables are managed by the OS/MMU, not autonomously by disks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA is set up by the kernel with IOMMUs/permissions on modern systems.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DMA moves data; it does not run arbitrary user programs on the device.

medium.prompt: Device drivers present a uniform interface to the kernel by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Translating OS requests (open/read/write/ioctl) into device-specific commands and interrupts.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Storing files only in the TLB

choices.label: C
choices.body: Eliminating the need for hardware interrupts

choices.label: D
choices.body: Running all devices at the same clock frequency

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Drivers hide hardware details while the kernel exposes a consistent I/O abstraction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Files live on persistent media; the TLB caches translations only.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Most devices still use interrupts or polling; drivers handle both.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clocking is hardware-dependent, not unified by drivers.

hard.prompt: Belady's anomaly demonstrates that with FIFO page replacement…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Increasing the number of frames can sometimes increase the number of page faults.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Fault rate is strictly decreasing in the number of frames

choices.label: C
choices.body: Optimal replacement is implementable in real hardware without future knowledge

choices.label: D
choices.body: LRU always performs worse than random replacement

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: FIFO lacks stack property; more memory does not guarantee fewer faults for all reference strings.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Belady's anomaly is exactly the failure of monotonic improvement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: OPT needs future reference information and is a theoretical benchmark.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: LRU is not the policy exhibiting Belady's anomaly in the classic result.

hard.prompt: The clock (second-chance) page replacement algorithm approximates LRU by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Scanning frames in a circular list and clearing reference bits before evicting.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Never using a hardware reference bit

choices.label: C
choices.body: Always evicting the most recently used page

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sorting frames by physical address each nanosecond

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: A set reference bit gives a page a second chance; cleared bits identify less recently used victims.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The algorithm depends on reference bits maintained by hardware/OS.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That would maximize faults, opposite of LRU's goal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Clock scans in ring order, not by sorting physical addresses continuously.

hard.prompt: Huge pages (large pages) can improve TLB coverage because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each TLB entry maps a larger virtual range, reducing misses for sequential/access-local workloads.

choices.label: B
choices.body: They prevent any process from sharing memory

choices.label: C
choices.body: They eliminate the need for page tables entirely

choices.label: D
choices.body: They guarantee zero internal fragmentation

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Fewer translations cover more bytes; the tradeoff is potential internal fragmentation and allocation granularity.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Shared mappings can use large pages when aligned and supported.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Page tables still exist; mappings are just coarser.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Larger granularity can increase internal fragmentation within a huge page.

hard.prompt: An inverted page table indexes entries by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Physical frame number, recording which virtual page (and process) occupies each frame.

choices.label: B
choices.body: File inode number and byte offset

choices.label: C
choices.body: Virtual page number only, one global table without process context

choices.label: D
choices.body: Thread ID and stack pointer exclusively

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Inverted tables scale with physical memory size but need hashing/collision handling to search by virtual address.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is filesystem addressing, not inverted page tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Classic multi-level tables index by virtual page; inverted flips the keying.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Address translation keys on virtual pages and process context, not stack pointers alone.

hard.prompt: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) improves security by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Encrypting every virtual page with a user-supplied password

choices.label: B
choices.body: Disabling all page faults

choices.label: C
choices.body: Running the kernel in user mode

choices.label: D
choices.body: Randomizing bases of stack, heap, and mappings so exploits cannot rely on fixed addresses.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Uncertainty in layout reduces success of return-oriented and buffer-overflow attacks that jump to known addresses.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ASLR changes placement, not per-page user encryption.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Faults still occur; ASLR only varies where regions are placed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Privilege levels are unchanged; layout is randomized.

hard.prompt: On a preemptive uniprocessor, Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) is optimal for…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Maximizing disk throughput on a RAID array

choices.label: B
choices.body: Guaranteeing zero page faults for all processes

choices.label: C
choices.body: Minimizing lateness among independent jobs with known deadlines, if total utilization ≤ 1.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Eliminating priority inversion without any locks

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: EDF dynamically prioritizes the job with the nearest deadline; overload (U > 1) still makes some jobs miss deadlines.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is storage scheduling, not uniprocessor real-time task scheduling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Memory behavior is unrelated to EDF's deadline optimality.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Inversion is a locking/scheduling interaction; EDF does not remove locks.

hard.prompt: Priority inheritance is used to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Disable preemption globally forever

choices.label: B
choices.body: Temporarily boost the priority of a lock holder so it finishes and releases the lock a high-priority waiter needs.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Permanently assign all threads to priority 0

choices.label: D
choices.body: Replace mutexes with busy-wait spinlocks only

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Boosting the holder reduces indirect blocking of high-priority tasks in priority inversion scenarios.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The system remains preemptive; only specific priorities are adjusted.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inheritance is temporary and targeted, not a global downgrade.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Inheritance complements proper locking; it does not eliminate mutexes.

hard.prompt: The many-to-one (M:1) user-thread model can perform poorly on multiprocessors because…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The kernel schedules only the single underlying kernel thread, limiting true parallel execution of user threads.

choices.label: B
choices.body: User threads cannot block on I/O

choices.label: C
choices.body: The kernel creates a new process for every mutex lock

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each user thread always gets its own hardware page table root

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Without a kernel thread per user thread, blocking one user thread can block all, and other cores may sit idle.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Blocking is exactly what exposes M:1 limitations.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Locks do not spawn processes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: M:1 shares one kernel context; separate page table roots are not per user thread by default.

hard.prompt: After fork() with copy-on-write, a write to a shared page in the parent typically causes the kernel to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Mark the page executable only in the child

choices.label: B
choices.body: Immediately terminate both parent and child

choices.label: C
choices.body: Flush the entire TLB and disk cache before any user instruction runs

choices.label: D
choices.body: Trap on write, allocate a new frame, copy the page, and remap the writer's page table entry.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Write protection on shared mappings triggers a COW fault handled by copying and updating permissions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: COW copies data pages; permissions follow policy for both address spaces.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: COW is a normal path, not a fatal error.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Only affected mappings/TLB entries need updating, not global flush of all caches.

hard.prompt: Log-structured file systems (LFS) optimize write performance by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Forbidding any form of buffering or caching

choices.label: B
choices.body: Storing data only in CPU registers

choices.label: C
choices.body: Updating every inode in place randomly across the disk

choices.label: D
choices.body: Appending all changes sequentially to a log and cleaning segments later.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Sequential writes match disk bandwidth; garbage collection reclaims space from old segments.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Buffer caches remain important; layout is what changes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: LFS still persists to block storage.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That resembles traditional layouts LFS tries to avoid for write cost.

hard.prompt: Copy-on-write tree structures (as in some snapshotting file systems) create snapshots by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Storing snapshots only in the TLB

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deleting all previous versions immediately on each write

choices.label: C
choices.body: Pointing new metadata roots at old blocks and copying only blocks that would be modified.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Duplicating the entire disk image eagerly on every read

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: COW trees share unchanged blocks between versions, paying space for divergent writes only.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Snapshots are persistent metadata/block structures, not TLB entries.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Snapshots retain old roots reachable for prior versions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Reads should remain cheap; duplication happens on write to shared blocks.

hard.prompt: Peterson's algorithm solves mutual exclusion for two threads using only loads/stores when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The CPU disables interrupts in user space without kernel help

choices.label: B
choices.body: More than two threads share one flag array of size 1

choices.label: C
choices.body: Shared variables (flag, turn) are accessed with proper memory ordering or on sequentially consistent hardware.

choices.label: D
choices.body: No shared variables exist

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Peterson's is a classic two-thread spin algorithm; correctness requires visible ordering of flag/turn updates.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: User programs cannot rely on interrupt masking alone on modern preemptive OSes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Peterson's is defined for two participants; more threads need different algorithms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The algorithm explicitly uses shared flag and turn variables.

hard.prompt: Mesa semantics for condition variables differ from Hoare semantics because Mesa…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Requires the waiter to re-check the condition after wakeup (while loop), not assume it holds immediately.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Forbids using while loops around wait

choices.label: C
choices.body: Automatically transfers monitor ownership to the signaled thread on signal

choices.label: D
choices.body: Guarantees the signaled thread runs before the signaler continues

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: With Mesa, signal/broadcast moves threads to ready; they compete and must verify predicates before proceeding.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Mesa-style code mandates re-testing conditions in a loop.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is closer to Hoare; Mesa does not hand over the monitor immediately.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Hoare gives stronger immediate handoff; Mesa does not.

hard.prompt: The ABA problem in lock-free programming occurs when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Virtual memory is disabled

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two threads never run concurrently

choices.label: C
choices.body: A location appears unchanged (A→B→A) but its structure was modified, fooling compare-and-swap checks.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All locks are implemented with semaphores only

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: CAS only compares values, not histories; reuse of the same pointer/value after pop/push can succeed incorrectly.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ABA is about pointer/value identity, not paging on/off.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: ABA arises under concurrency with reuse of nodes/values.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: ABA is specific to lock-free CAS-based structures.

hard.prompt: A memory barrier (fence) in concurrent code ensures…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Heap allocations require no synchronization

choices.label: B
choices.body: Page replacement chooses OPT automatically

choices.label: C
choices.body: Ordering constraints so some loads/stores cannot be reordered across the fence by compiler or CPU.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All threads run on the same CPU core

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Barriers publish/consume shared data safely on weak memory models.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Allocation and memory ordering are separate concerns.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: OPT is unrelated to CPU memory ordering fences.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Barriers matter especially when threads run on different cores with reordering.

hard.prompt: Deadlock prevention by breaking 'hold and wait' typically requires…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Granting every request immediately without checking safety

choices.label: B
choices.body: Allowing circular wait chains to form freely

choices.label: C
choices.body: Processes to request all needed resources atomically before starting (or release all before new requests).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Ignoring maximum claim vectors in the banker algorithm

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: If a process cannot hold partial allocations while waiting, circular wait chains cannot form via held resources.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Immediate unsafe grants cause deadlock rather than prevent it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would not prevent deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Claims are central to avoidance algorithms, not this prevention tactic.

hard.prompt: Deadlock detection with multiple instances of resources often uses…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A wait-for graph or reduction of the resource-allocation state to see if a safe sequence exists.

choices.label: B
choices.body: ASLR entropy values

choices.label: C
choices.body: TLB hit rate measurements

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only the FCFS CPU scheduling rule

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Detection examines whether processes can finish with current availability, similar in spirit to safety checks.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Security randomization does not detect resource deadlocks.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: TLB statistics measure translation performance, not deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: FCFS is unrelated to resource deadlock detection.

hard.prompt: An I/O scheduler elevator (e.g., SCAN) reduces seek cost on disks by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Caching virtual addresses in the TLB

choices.label: B
choices.body: Issuing every request in random order always

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disabling DMA transfers entirely

choices.label: D
choices.body: Serving requests in one direction along the disk until the end, then reversing.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Directional scanning batches nearby cylinder requests, improving throughput versus pure FCFS on rotating media.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: TLBs are for memory translation, not disk arm scheduling.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Random ordering increases seeks; elevators sort spatially.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: DMA and arm scheduling are independent optimizations.

hard.prompt: Spurious wakeups on condition variables imply that correct code should…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Assume the predicate is true without checking

choices.label: B
choices.body: Disable the scheduler entirely

choices.label: C
choices.body: Never call signal or broadcast

choices.label: D
choices.body: Re-test the waited-on predicate in a loop after returning from wait.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Threads may wake without the condition holding; loops prevent proceeding on false wakeups.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That races with concurrent changes and spurious wakeups.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Scheduling continues; waiters must verify state.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Signaling is still required; callers must handle spurious wakeups.

hard.prompt: Thrashing in a demand-paging system is best described as…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A filesystem journaling mode

choices.label: B
choices.body: A state where no page faults occur

choices.label: C
choices.body: Optimal CPU-bound throughput with infinite frames

choices.label: D
choices.body: Excessive paging where CPU time is dominated by fault handling and little useful work completes.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: When the working set does not fit, processes fault constantly, queue grows, and performance collapses.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Thrashing is a memory overcommit phenomenon, not a log mode.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Thrashing involves very high fault rates, not zero faults.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Enough frames prevent thrashing; infinite memory is not the definition.
